design_detail: Retrospective single-centre review of the case files of all standard medicolegal autopsies performed in 2016–2021 at the Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Regional Autopsy Center (AHWFBRAC), which provides medicolegal autopsies for 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038) and kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021. Of 6,248 files, 2,956 were included after excluding decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury and intentional (suicidal) overdoses. Each case was classified twice: (1) suspicion of a drug-related death before autopsy, from the preliminary report of death and investigative information (drug paraphernalia at the scene, current or prior substance use disorder, prior overdoses) that the centre's medicolegal death investigators obtained from county medical examiners with standardized questions; and (2) the final cause of death after full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology, as determined by the assigned forensic pathologist. Results are a 2×2 table with sensitivity, specificity and the authors' own false-positive and false-negative rates. Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case-file and certificate studies; the accuracy statistics are recorded as the paper's.
can_establish: How often, at one regional autopsy centre in 2016–2021, deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug-related ended with a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology (265 of 2,719), and how often deaths not suspected ended with a drug-related cause (115 of 237).
cannot_establish: How many deaths external examination with toxicology but without autopsy would actually have put down to drugs wrongly (the 265 'false positives' include deaths with negative toxicology, which toxicology alone would have flagged, and the split is not reported); whether the final causes were right (the pathologist's determination is the reference, and illicit drugs found were treated as at least contributing unless a catastrophic Adelson class I process was present); or the figures elsewhere, for intentional overdoses, children or deaths with obvious injury, which were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Records: case files of all standard medicolegal autopsies performed at AHWFBRAC from 2016 to 2021 (p. 189, Methods/Materials 1st paragraph; p. 190, Results 1st paragraph). The centre served 33 western North Carolina counties and performed full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021 while other offices had moved to external examination with toxicology specimens (p. 189, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury, and deaths from intentional suicidal overdose of prescription or illicit drugs. Suicidal overdoses were excluded because they were already identified as intentional at referral and because, the authors say, many did not meet the study's criteria for a likely drug-related death (p. 189, Methods/Materials 1st paragraph). The number excluded for each reason is not reported; 3,292 of 6,248 files were excluded in all (editors' arithmetic).
sample.demographics: Not reported. Age and sex were extracted from the files (p. 189, Methods/Materials 2nd paragraph) but are not presented.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). No missing-data handling is reported.
sample.selection_effects: One regional centre; only autopsied deaths enter. Excluding obvious injuries and suicides removes groups in which the final cause would often differ from, or agree with, drug suspicion. Only 237 included deaths were not suspected of drug involvement and only 387 had a non-drug final cause, out of 6,248 autopsies, so most autopsies without drug involvement were excluded (presumably as obvious injuries or minors; counts by exclusion criterion are not given). The authors note that the sample reflects western North Carolina only (p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The classification under test is suspicion of a drug-related death before autopsy, from the preliminary report of death (a brief report available at the time of autopsy) and investigative information gathered by the centre's medicolegal death investigators from county medical examiners with standardized questions; the criteria were drug paraphernalia at the scene (needles, syringes, cut straws, pill crushers, burnt foil, rolled papers, baggies with residue), current or prior substance use disorder, and prior overdoses (p. 189, Methods/Materials 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). How the criteria were combined, who classified each case for the study, and whether that classification was made without knowledge of the final cause are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Substances found in blood or other tissues were tabulated from the toxicology reports (p. 189, Methods/Materials 3rd paragraph); Figure 2 gives the yearly share of drug-related deaths in which heroin, fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine were 'involved' (p. 191). Combinations are not analysed.

comparison.controls: Within-series comparison: deaths suspected and not suspected before autopsy, each set against the final cause after full autopsy and toxicology (Table 1, p. 190). There is no comparison with deaths certified without autopsy and no independent review of the final causes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Case characteristics that could affect both suspicion and final cause (age, sex, known disease, decomposition, interval to autopsy) are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Final cause of death from the autopsy and toxicology reports, as determined by the forensic pathologist assigned the case (p. 189, Methods/Materials 3rd paragraph; p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph). Toxicology: specimens sent to a forensic toxicology laboratory that screened for over-the-counter, prescription and illicit drugs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and gas chromatography with nitrogen-phosphorus detection after base/neutral extraction, and by targeted liquid chromatography with high-resolution (quadrupole-Orbitrap) mass spectrometry, with confirmation and quantitation by LC-MS-MS; point-of-care urine screens were not used (pp. 189–190, Methods/Materials 4th paragraph). Specimen types, sampling sites, the share of cases tested and concentrations are not reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors assume the assigned pathologist's cause of death is correct, and treat illicit drugs present at death as at least contributing to death except when an Adelson class I natural or traumatic process (catastrophic, fatal regardless of other conditions) was found (p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph; p. 191, Results 2nd paragraph). The reference therefore partly incorporates the investigative information on which the suspicion under test was based, and it counts the presence of illicit drugs as contribution.
outcomes.operationalization: False positive: high suspicion at referral, but toxicology negative, or illicit substances present with other significant non-toxicologic findings that explain the death. False negative: very low or no suspicion at referral, but toxicology showed a drug toxicity as the cause of death without significant autopsy findings (p. 190, Methods/Materials 5th paragraph). Formulas: sensitivity TP/(TP+FN); specificity TN/(TN+FP); false-positive rate FP/all suspected cases (that is, 1 minus the positive predictive value, not 1 minus specificity); false-negative rate FN/all final drug-related cases. The authors note that these definitions are not universal.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: four descriptive proportions and yearly drug shares; no hypothesis test is reported, although drug trends are called significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The classification was made retrospectively from files that contained the autopsy and toxicology reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 190): suspected 2,719 (final drug-related 2,454; not drug-related 265); not suspected 237 (drug-related 115; not 122). Reported: sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%, false-negative rate 4.48%, false-positive rate 9.75% (p. 190, Results 1st paragraph); all four reproduce from Table 1 (editors' arithmetic). No intervals are reported. Editors' calculations (Wilson 95% intervals): false-positive rate as defined, 265/2,719 = 9.75% (8.7 to 10.9); positive predictive value 2,454/2,719 = 90.25% (89.1 to 91.3); share of the 237 deaths not suspected that had a drug-related final cause, 115/237 = 48.5% (42.2 to 54.9); conventional false-positive rate (1 minus specificity), 265/387 = 68.5% (63.7 to 72.9); overall agreement, 2,576/2,956 = 87.1% (85.9 to 88.3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The 265 false positives are not split into deaths with negative toxicology and deaths with drugs present but another cause, although only the second kind would be missed by external examination with toxicology; the alternative causes are given only as examples (p. 191). Age and sex were extracted but not reported, and the exclusions are not counted by reason.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The main proportions rest on 2,719 suspected and 387 non-drug cases; figures for the 237 deaths not suspected are less precise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At one regional centre, 9.75% of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related had a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology. The share that external examination with toxicology would have put down to drugs wrongly is smaller by an unreported amount, because the 265 include deaths with negative toxicology. In the other direction, 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) ended with a drug-related cause.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states only the purpose and gives no results. The Results say investigators could “correctly predict” a suspected drug-related fatality in more than 95% of cases (p. 190, Results 2nd paragraph), but 95.5% is the sensitivity: 90.3% of suspected deaths were drug-related and overall agreement was 87.1% (editors' calculation). The Results and Conclusions present the almost-10% false-positive rate as the share of cases that could have been misclassified if only investigation, toxicology and external examination had been done (p. 190, Results 2nd paragraph; p. 192, Conclusions), which overstates it, since toxicology-negative deaths are included. The Conclusions add that the data are informational and not meant to sway offices toward one practice (p. 192). Rises in fentanyl and methamphetamine are called significant without any test (p. 191, Results 3rd paragraph).

timeline.event: Nashelsky and Lawrence, accuracy of cause-of-death determination without forensic autopsy (cited as reference 21 among reasons offices use external examinations; not read for this card).

Fryer et al.: in a selected group of high-risk referrals, external examination, toxicology and/or post-mortem CT could cut standard autopsies by two-thirds (reference 20, as summarized in the Discussion, p. 191).
Andrew and Duval: 11% to 13% of suspected drug-related deaths had toxicology that explained nothing and another cause (reference 18, as summarized, p. 191).

Dye et al.: three pathologists given history, scene, external examination and toxicology, without internal findings, classified cause and manner correctly in 75% to 80% of 60 cases selected from 629 (reference 19, as summarized, p. 191; on the project's list as #28, not read).
NAME position paper: autopsy recommended whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death; cited by this study as current best practice (reference 14).
This study: 265 of 2,719 suspected drug-related deaths (9.75%) had a non-drug final cause after full autopsy at one North Carolina centre, 2016–2021.

replication.where_it_stands: A single-centre study with no direct replication. The two earlier studies it summarizes report broadly similar magnitudes by different designs (11% to 13% with another cause; 20% to 25% misclassified without internal examination), but they are second-hand here. It is the only study on the project's list that counts, in drug deaths, how often full autopsy overturned a suspected drug death; read with the NAME position paper (Davis et al., 2020), which recommends autopsy without quantifying the error it prevents.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 189, first-page footnote).
funding.affiliations_note: First author a pathology resident (Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center); second an associate professor, Wake Forest University School of Medicine; third a senior biostatistician in that school's Department of Biostatistics and Data Science (p. 189). The NAME position paper that recommends autopsy for suspected overdose deaths (Davis et al., 2020, p. 152) lists a panel member with the same name and institution (Jerri L. McLemore, Department of Pathology, Wake Forest School of Medicine). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study in several offices in which, for every suspected drug-related death, a certifier records a cause of death from scene investigation, external examination and full toxicology before the autopsy, without seeing its findings, and an independent panel then assigns the cause after full autopsy; reporting separately the deaths with drugs present but another cause, and including intentional overdoses and deaths with injuries.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All autopsies of a regional centre serving 33 counties, but only autopsied deaths in one region; the target, suspected drug deaths certified without autopsy elsewhere, is wider.

All files for 2016–2021 were reviewed, but 3,292 of 6,248 were excluded with no count by reason, and suicidal overdoses were excluded partly because they did not fit the study's own suspicion criteria.
2,719 suspected and 387 non-drug cases give precise main proportions; the 237 deaths not suspected give wider intervals.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: No age, sex, manner of death, interval to autopsy or decomposition by group; the final causes of the 265 false positives are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Table 1 accounts for all 2,956 included cases. Figure 1's regional total for 2016–2021 (2,605, editors' sum) differs from the 2,569 final drug-related cases, without explanation.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Full autopsy with comprehensive toxicology interpreted by a forensic pathologist is the best available reference, but it is assumed correct, it counts illicit drugs present as contributing unless a class I process is found, and the 'false positive' category merges negative toxicology with drugs present and another cause.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: How the suspicion criteria were combined, who classified the cases and whether they knew the final cause are not reported; many pathologists over six years, with no agreement measure.

Counts and proportions reproduce from Table 1, but there are no intervals, the false-positive rate is not the conventional one, the verbal definition of the false-negative rate contradicts its formula, sensitivity is described as prediction accuracy, and trends are called significant without a test.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case-file studies, because the figure the site needs is a proportion: the share of suspected drug deaths that full autopsy assigned to another cause. The paper presents it as test accuracy; a QUADAS-2 reading would flag the same weaknesses (a retrospective classification of suspicion with unknown blinding, and a reference standard that incorporates the investigation behind that suspicion and counts illicit drugs present as contributing). Editors' summary: moderate risk of bias as a description of this series; as an estimate of what external examination with toxicology would misattribute, 9.75% is an upper bound of unknown distance. Citable for: at one North Carolina centre in 2016–2021, 265 of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related (9.75%) had a non-drug final cause after full autopsy and toxicology, including some with negative toxicology; 115 of 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) had a drug-related final cause; the examples of alternative causes; and the rule that illicit drugs found counted as contributing unless a class I process was present. Not citable for: the misclassification rate of certification without autopsy as such, rates in other regions, suicides or children, or the accuracy of post-mortem drug levels (none are reported).

key_findings.finding: The Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Regional Autopsy Center provides medicolegal autopsies for 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038) and performed full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021, while other offices had adopted external examination with toxicology specimens; the study asked whether external examination with comprehensive toxicology alone missed disease or injury that would change the cause of death.

Of 6,248 autopsy case files from 2016–2021, 2,956 met the inclusion criteria after excluding decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury, and deaths from intentional suicidal overdose of prescription or illicit drugs.
key_findings.note: Exclusions are not counted by reason; 3,292 files excluded in all (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Pre-autopsy suspicion came from the preliminary report of death and from information that the centre's medicolegal death investigators obtained from county medical examiners with standardized questions; a likely drug-related death was judged from drug paraphernalia at the scene, current or prior substance use disorder, and prior overdoses.

Table 1: of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related, 2,454 had a drug-related final cause and 265 did not; of 237 deaths not suspected, 115 had a drug-related final cause and 122 did not (column totals 2,569 drug-related and 387 not; 2,956 in all).

Reported accuracy: sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%, false-negative rate 4.48% and false-positive rate 9.75%, where the false-positive rate is false positives divided by all suspected cases (265/2,719) and the false-negative rate is false negatives divided by all final drug-related cases (115/2,569).
key_findings.note: All four reproduce from Table 1 (editors' arithmetic). No confidence intervals are given; the editors' Wilson 95% interval for 9.75% is 8.7% to 10.9%.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculations from Table 1: positive predictive value of suspicion 90.25% (2,454/2,719); share of deaths not suspected that had a drug-related final cause 48.5% (115/237; 95% interval 42.2% to 54.9%); conventional false-positive rate, 1 minus specificity, 68.5% (265/387); overall agreement 87.1% (2,576/2,956).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Wilson intervals); none of these figures is printed in the paper.

key_findings.finding: A false positive was defined as a death with high suspicion at referral whose toxicology was negative, or in which illicit substances were present but other significant non-toxicologic findings explained the death; the paper does not report how many of the 265 fell into each kind.

Alternative causes found in suspected drug deaths were Adelson class I processes, catastrophic and fatal regardless of other conditions; examples given are pulmonary emboli, a ruptured gastric ulcer, a ruptured berry aneurysm without stimulants in the body, and a compressive subdural haematoma with a manner of homicide.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 190, right column; examples on p. 191)
key_findings.note: Examples only; no counts by cause.

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: the cause of death determined by the assigned forensic pathologist was assumed correct; illicit drugs present at the time of death were taken as at least contributing to death except in deaths with class I natural or traumatic processes; the sample reflects western North Carolina only.

Toxicology screened for over-the-counter, prescription and illicit drugs by GC-MS, GC-NPD and targeted high-resolution LC-MS, with confirmation and quantitation by LC-MS-MS; point-of-care qualitative urine drug screens were not used. Specimen types and sites are not stated and no concentrations are reported.

Figure 2 gives the yearly percentage of drug-related deaths in the region in which each of four illicit drugs was 'involved', 2016 to 2021: heroin 23, 19, 18, 20, 10, 5; fentanyl 10, 29, 44, 51, 54, 77; methamphetamine 13, 16, 25, 23, 30, 40; cocaine 17, 19, 18, 21, 15, 22. The text says fentanyl and, to a lesser degree, methamphetamine increased significantly and cocaine stayed consistent.
key_findings.note: Values are printed as data labels in the figure image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; they are not in the PDF text layer). The denominator of each percentage and the meaning of 'involved' (detected, or listed as a cause) are not stated; no test is reported.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 gives the yearly number of drug-related deaths at the centre, 2016 to 2021: 316, 336, 369, 334, 530 and 720; and nationally: 63,600, 70,237, 67,367, 62,172, 93,665 and 107,622.
key_findings.note: Data labels in the figure image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; not in the text layer). No source is given for the national values; the regional values sum to 2,605 (editors' arithmetic), not the 2,569 final drug-related cases of Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Studies summarized in the Discussion: one found 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths had toxicology that explained nothing and another cause (Andrew and Duval); in another, three pathologists blind to internal findings determined cause and manner correctly in 75% to 80% of 60 cases selected from 629 (Dye et al.); a third found external examination, toxicology and/or post-mortem CT could cut standard autopsies by two-thirds in a selected high-risk group (Fryer et al.).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the primary studies were not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the false-positive rate was almost 10%, enough cases to matter for misclassification; that post-mortem CT might reduce the risk if offices had access to it; and that the data are meant as information, not to sway offices toward one practice.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says 2,569 cases were suspected to be drug-related at referral and 387 were not; Table 1 shows 2,719 suspected and 237 not suspected, and 2,569 and 387 are the totals of final drug-related and non-drug causes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group sizes must be taken from Table 1; the printed rates reproduce only from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The false-negative rate is defined in words as the proportion of negative preliminary findings that were true overdose deaths (115/237 = 48.5%, editors' calculation), but the formula and the printed value use all final drug-related cases as the denominator (115/2,569 = 4.48%). The false-positive rate (265/2,719) is 1 minus the positive predictive value, not 1 minus specificity (265/387 = 68.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels invite misreading. The 4.48% hides that nearly half of the deaths not suspected were drug-related; the 9.75% is not a conventional false-positive rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the investigators correctly predicted a suspected drug-related fatality before autopsy in more than 95% of cases, which is the sensitivity read as overall accuracy; the timing of suspicion is described as 'at autopsy' for the four groups but 'upon referral' in the definitions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Overall agreement was 87.1% and the positive predictive value 90.3% (editors' calculations); the 95% figure should not be cited as prediction accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: The false-positive category combines deaths with negative toxicology and deaths with drugs present but another cause, and the split is not reported, although the paper presents the whole 9.75% as the deaths that could have been misclassified without autopsy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is an upper bound for what external examination with toxicology would misattribute; the true share cannot be recovered from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1's regional counts sum to 2,605, against 2,569 final drug-related deaths in Table 1, and its national counts have no stated source; the 2019 national value (62,172) differs from the 70,630 for 2019 that Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025, p. 542) give from NCHS data, while the 2017 and 2018 values agree with Davis et al. (2020, p. 152) and Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's numbers should not be cited as official counts; the regional difference may reflect the excluded intentional overdoses or minors, which the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's trends are called significant with no test, heroin is said to have declined steadily though 2019 (20%) is above 2018 (18%), and the denominators of the percentages are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The yearly shares may be cited as descriptive figures from the figure labels, not as tested trends.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction gives national deaths 'in 2021 alone' (more than 100,000, over 70,000 involving synthetic opioids) from a CDC press release dated 17 November 2021 (reference 12), before the year had ended.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure refers to a 12-month period other than calendar 2021; cite national counts from NCHS reports, not from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states the purpose but reports no results, and the methods do not say how the suspicion criteria were combined or who classified the cases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study cannot be judged from its abstract; the classification step cannot be reproduced.

No supplement, correction or comment is named or in the files. Read by AI reader 295. The reference record agrees with the PDF (title, three authors, year, volume, issue, pages).
